title: rail-saturation-prefetch-seqlen-mix-fieldnotes
content:
Purpose:
Quick lab notes for an investigation into how memory-rail (channel) saturation interacts with prefetch heuristics under mixed sequence-length workloads. The goal is to identify a compact set of signals we can surface in telemetry and a short mitigation checklist (tunable knobs + fallback) to reduce tail latency and read-amplification when NVMe paging or PCIe->DRAM contention flares.

Background / motivation:
- We see intermittent tail latency spikes correlated with increased NVMe activity during multi-tenant spikes. Suspect cross-rail bandwidth contention exacerbates KV cache miss storm impact.
- Recent production traces (sample attached in linked_artifacts) show 95th/99th token latency jumps when short-chat traffic coexists with longer-completion batch jobs.
- Prior experiments focused on eviction policy; this probe focuses on prefetch timing and whether aggressive prefetch crediting causes bank-saturation that amplifies paging IO.

Hypotheses:
1) Aggressive prefetch windows combined with uneven per-rail DMA scheduling leads to burst reads that oversubscribe a small number of memory channels and NVMe queues, producing long queuing times and read-amplification.
2) Mixed seqlen mixes create hotspots: long-seq requests hold KV pages in-flight longer, while short-seq bursts generate prefetch churn that forces eviction/prefetch thrash on the same physical pages.
3) Tighter prefetch pacing (credit-bucket smoothing) will reduce 99th percentile latency without materially increasing average latency or miss-rate for majority workloads.

Experimental setup:
- Hardware: 8x A100-equivalent with 8 memory channels, NVMe pool (4x7000-series) in RAID0 used in lab, PCIe gen4.
- Runtime: local build; prefetch tunables exposed: PREFETCH_WINDOW_MS (10..200), PREFETCH_BATCH_SZ (1..64), PREFETCH_CREDIT_BUCKET (0..1000), PREFETCH_STRIDE_CAP (0..4).
- Workloads: synthetic traces replayed over 4 hours with 2 phases: phase A (short-chat mix: 70% reqs seqlen 32, 30% seqlen 64 at 200 qps) and phase B (long-worker mix: 50% seqlen 512, 30% seqlen 128, 20% short at 100 qps). Interleave A/B to create contention.
- Measurement: per-rail bandwidth, NVMe queue depth, miss rate, eviction churn, tokens/sec, p50/ p95/ p99 token latency. Also collected sampled KV page access traces (timestamped) for a few runs.

Key observations (abridged):
Run 1 (baseline - PREFETCH_WINDOW_MS=50, CREDIT=500, BATCH_SZ=16):
- p50 stable, p95 1.6x baseline, p99 spikes up to 4x during handoffs from A->B.
- NVMe queue depth shows synchronized bursts aligning with prefetch windows, channels 2 and 3 hit sustained 94% utilization while others sat at 40% (rail skew).
- Eviction churn increased by ~22% during bursts; read-amplification (bytes read / useful bytes) ~1.9x.

Run 2 (reduce window -> 20ms, credit 250, batch 8):
- p99 reduces by ~35% vs Run1; NVMe queue depth smoother, less per-rail skew (max 75%).
- Miss rate slightly higher (~3%) but overall tokens/sec unaffected.
- Read-amplification down to ~1.3x.

Run 3 (aggressive window 150ms, batch 32):
- p99 catastrophically worse; sustained NVMe storm; single-run outage-like tail events observed.
- Kernel traces show sustained DMA bursts with limited interleaving across channels (cause: sequential prefetch requests mapping to same memory interleaving pattern).

Run 4 (enable stride cap=1 + credit bucket smoothing):
- p99 improved to near Run2 but miss-rate decrease recovered; per-rail utilization balanced better.
- Eviction churn reduced relative to baseline.

Micro-trace analysis notes:
- Prefetch requests often target contiguous page ranges aligned to 2MB boundaries; on our machine this maps frequently to channel 2/3 for model shard layout used in this test. Little randomness in page assignment -> high skew.
- Long seqlen requests tend to hold KV page locks longer (waiting on generation), so prefetches from short requests race to bring different pages into the same rails, causing thrash and SSD read re-reads as evicted pages get requested again.

Operational telemetry signals to add (minimal set):
1) per-rail instantaneous BW (1s and 10s windows) with relative skew score (max/min).
2) prefetch-credit-debt gauge (how many pending prefetched pages vs steady-state).
3) eviction-churn-rate (evictions/sec normalized by resident_set).
4) read-amplification ratio (bytes_read / bytes_served) per 5m window.
5) NVMe avg queue latency and QD distribution.

Quick mitigations (short-term):
- Default PREFETCH_WINDOW_MS -> 25ms for multi-tenant hosts; reduce PREFETCH_BATCH_SZ to 8.
- Enable PREFETCH_STRIDE_CAP=1 by default on instances with <X shards and for models with sequential KV layout.
- Soft-cap per-rail inflight prefetch ops: if rail_skew_score > 1.6, throttle new prefetches on heavy rails and redistribute to cooler rails (experimentally reduces peaks).

Longer-term ideas:
- Page-mapping randomizer (cheap XOR) at allocation time for KV pages to reduce static mapping hotspotting for commonly-used model shard layout. Would require validation for cache affinity losses.
- Rail-aware prefetch planner: use compact allocation that staggers contiguous prefetches to different channels intentionally. Needs cooperation with the allocator/kernels.
- Admission control: identify long-held KV locks (long-seqlen requests) and prefer read-through for short-seq low-latency clients rather than prefetch for large ranges.

Open questions / next steps:
- Need to validate whether rail-skew is mostly an artifact of our lab HW mapping or also present in cloud instances across different vendors (NVIDIA A100 vs H100 vs AMD). Run same trace on H100-like nodes.
- Quantify the trade-off between slight miss-rate increase and tail-latency improvement across a wider set of models and shardings. Create matrix: model (Llama-2-70B, Mistral-22B, Redwood-Base), shard_count (4,8,16), prefetch knobs.
- Evaluate page-randomization perf impact for high-throughput steady-state workloads.

Notes to reviewers:
- Attached sample traces in linked_artifacts correspond to Run1 and Run3. Run4 contains more detailed kernel DMA timelines if you want to step through.
- This doc is intentionally a lab scratchpad — some sections are messy; suggestions for additional telemetry or quick experimental knob to try are welcome.
- If we agree on short-term defaults, I can open a small PR to change platform defaults and add the telemetry panels (per-rail skew score + read-amplification) to the per-cluster dashboard.

Experiment log (timestamps):
- 2024-12-06: baseline capture + initial run1/2/3.
- 2024-12-12: reproduce on different host, confirmed rail skew persists.
- 2025-01-15: run4 (stride cap + credit smoothing) with improved telemetry.

Concluding takeaway (TL;DR):
Aggressive prefetching + deterministic page-to-rail mapping can create high rail-skew and NVMe queue storms under mixed seqlen traffic. Conservative prefetch windows, smaller batches, credit smoothing and a small stride cap are effective quick mitigations to cut 99th percentile token latency and read-amplification with tolerable miss-rate increases.

-- Aisha
